- NEVER run 'python', 'python3', or any interpreter of the source. Only run the executable, and 'node' for your own scratch calculations.
- Use bash. A useful baseline invocation that always succeeds:
  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable --a 'Test123' --b '2' --c 'x' --d 'y' --e '3' --f 1 --g 2; echo "RC=$?"
- Vary ONLY the argument(s) you are probing; keep the others at safe values so the line you care about is the one that changes.
- Always capture the exit code, and capture stdout and stderr SEPARATELY (e.g. > /tmp/out 2> /tmp/err; echo $?).
- To see raw bytes of output when in doubt, pipe through 'od -c' or 'cat -A'.
- Line 4 echoes the exact raw bytes of --c, so line 4 is your microscope for how Python renders a bytes object.
- Run MANY probes (30+). Be systematic and exhaustive. Report ONLY what you actually observed, with the exact command and exact output. Mark anything you infer but did not directly observe as unverified.


YOUR JOB: adversarial verification. Another agent probed area "bytes-repr" and claims these rules about /workspace/dataset/test20_executable.
Your default assumption is that each rule is WRONG, over-general, or missing an edge case.

For EACH rule below, design and run FRESH commands (do not just repeat their evidence command) that would EXPOSE it if false. Try boundary values, empty values, and combinations. Then judge.

RULES TO ATTACK:
[1] rule: Every bytes-valued line (lines 1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,10,11,12) is rendered as CPython `bytes.__repr__`: the single lowercase ASCII letter `b` (0x62), immediately followed by the opening delimiter quote, the escaped body, then the same closing quote. No space after `b`, no `bytearray(...)` wrapper, no `...` truncation ever.
    their evidence: /workspace/dataset/test20_executable --a 'Test123' --b '2' --c 'x' --d 'y' --e '3' --f 1 --g 2 -> lines: b'4CVtFLcCiv' / b'\x01' / b'EYVuQ4z' / b'x' / b'2' / 1 / b'36' / b'\x02' / b'3' / b'BXvDbH' / b'\x01' / b'2'  (RC=0). od -c of that stdout starts: b   '   4   C   V   t ...
[2] rule: Delimiter selection: count occurrences of 0x27 (single quote) as sq and 0x22 (double quote) as dq in the byte string. If sq>0 AND dq==0, the delimiter is the double quote `"`. In ALL other cases (sq==0, or dq>0 regardless of sq) the delimiter is the single quote `'`. Relative counts do not matter, only zero vs nonzero.
    their evidence: --c "'" -> b"'" ; --c '\"' -> b'"' ; --c 'a'\''b"c' -> b'a\'b"c' ; --c 'plain' -> b'plain' ; --b '213fka' (bytes 27 27 27 27) -> b"''''" ; --b '213fkV' (bytes 27 27 27 22) -> b'\'\'\'"' ; --b '211yxm' (bytes 27 22 22 22) -> b'\'"""'
[3] rule: Per-byte escaping, applied independently to each byte in order: (1) byte == delimiter code point -> backslash + that quote char; (2) byte == 0x5c -> two backslashes `\\`; (3) byte == 0x09 -> `\t`; (4) byte == 0x0a -> `\n`; (5) byte == 0x0d -> `\r`; (6) byte < 0x20 or byte >= 0x7f -> `\x` + exactly two LOWERCASE zero-padded hex digits; (7) otherwise (0x20..0x7e) -> the literal ASCII character.
    their evidence: Differential test: 45 pseudo-random byte strings (1-12 bytes, biased toward 0x00,0x09,0x0a,0x0d,0x22,0x27,0x5c,0x1f,0x20,0x7e,0x7f,0x80,0xff) were b58-encoded in node, fed as --b, and line 2 compared to a node implementation of exactly this rule: PASS=45 FAIL=0
[4] rule: The quote character that is NOT the delimiter is emitted literally, unescaped. So with a single-quote delimiter a 0x22 byte prints as a bare `"`, and with a double-quote delimiter a 0x27 byte prints as a bare `'`.
    their evidence: --b '3cf' (bytes 22 5c) -> b'"\\'  (double quote literal inside single-quoted literal) ; --b '3zj' (bytes 27 5c) -> b"'\\" (single quote literal inside double-quoted literal) ; --b '3bk' (bytes 22 27) -> b'"\''
